title: "What TROP can and cannot do"
description: >
  The limits of the method and of this package in plain words, and good
  practice for an analysis.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
source("_setup.R")
```

::: {.key-points}
Key points

- The authors suggest TROP or synthetic difference in differences as a simple
  choice for panel data. No method works for every data set.
- The triple robustness result has a proof only for a block design.
- The bootstrap interval is reliable only with many treated units.
- In our simulation with larger trends for the treated units, TROP reduced the
  bias, but some bias stayed.
- fasttrop cannot use covariates.
:::

## What TROP can do

- Estimate the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) for block,
  staggered, and general designs, with the local method.
- Use panels in which some outcomes are not in the data. The fits do not use
  these cells.
- Adapt to the data. Cross-validation uses the data to set the tuning
  parameters. They control the unit weights, the time weights, and the
  low-rank term.
- Give a standard error and a confidence interval with a unit bootstrap.

## The limits of the method

### The triple robustness result has a proof only for a block design

The paper gives a limit on the bias of TROP (Theorem 5.1). This limit is the
reason for the name "triply robust". The proof is only for a block design, in
which all treated units start the treatment in the same period and stay
treated.

fasttrop also calculates estimates for staggered and general designs, but it
gives a warning message. For these designs, the estimate is available, but
the triple robustness result has no proof. The proof also uses fixed weights,
and TROP selects its weights from the data.

### The bootstrap interval is reliable only with many treated units

The paper says that its bootstrap is correct only with many treated units.
fasttrop gives a warning message for a panel with fewer than five treated
units. Five or more treated units do not make the interval reliable. With one
or two treated units, for example one state with a new law, the interval can
be wrong.

In our simulation A, a random draw selected 10 treated units. The normal
intervals of TROP had a coverage of 92.5% to 94%, near the target of 95%. In
simulation B, the selection used the trend of the units. There, the same
intervals had a coverage of only 47.5% to 70%.

fasttrop also keeps the tuning parameters fixed in the bootstrap. Thus, the
interval does not include the variation that comes from the selection of the
tuning parameters.

### Different trends can leave some bias

TROP calculates the outcomes without the treatment from the untreated cells.
In our simulation B, the selection favored units with larger trends. TROP
reduced the bias, but some bias stayed. This result gives no general rule
about which weights can remove a bias. Under the assumptions of the paper, a
model without bias can also remove it.

In simulation A, a random draw selects the treated units. In simulation B, the
selection favors the units with the largest trends. The true effect is 1 in
both simulations.

```{r bias-fig, fig.asp = 0.5, fig.cap = "Bias of three estimators, with 200 simulated panels in each simulation. In simulation A, a random draw selects the treated units. In simulation B, the selection favors the units with the largest trends. The bars show two Monte Carlo standard errors.", fig.alt = "A dot chart in two panels. In simulation A, the bias is -0.10 for TWFE, -0.04 for TROP local, and -0.03 for TROP global. In simulation B, the bias is 1.20 for TWFE, 0.64 for TROP local, and 0.37 for TROP global."}
read_summary <- function(design) {
  utils::read.csv(system.file("validation", sprintf("known-truth-summary-%s.csv", design),
                              package = "fasttrop"))
}
sims <- rbind(read_summary("A"), read_summary("B"))
sims$method <- factor(sims$method, levels = c("global", "local", "twfe"),
                      labels = c("TROP global", "TROP local", "TWFE"))
sims$simulation <- factor(sims$design, levels = c("A", "B"),
                          labels = c("A: random selection", "B: selection on the trend"))
sims$is_trop <- sims$method != "TWFE"

ggplot(sims, aes(bias, method, colour = is_trop)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ft_col[["muted"]], linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = bias - 2 * mc_se_bias, xmax = bias + 2 * mc_se_bias),
                 height = 0.25, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 3.6) +
  geom_text(aes(x = bias + 2 * mc_se_bias + 0.05, label = sprintf("%.2f", bias)),
            hjust = 0, size = 3.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~simulation, nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = ft_col[["teal"]], `FALSE` = ft_col[["coral"]]),
                      guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1), expand = expansion(add = c(0.05, 0.3))) +
  labs(x = "Bias (the true effect is 1)", y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.spacing = unit(2, "lines"))
```

In simulation A, each bias is small, and each one is less than three Monte
Carlo standard errors from zero. In simulation B, TWFE has a large bias. TROP
removes approximately half of this bias with the local method and two thirds
with the global method, but some bias stays. The intervals in simulation B
also have a coverage below 95%. The article
[How we checked fasttrop](validation.html) shows the saved results for TWFE
and the two TROP methods.

### General designs assume no carryover

In a general design, the treatment stops for some units. The estimator then
uses the cells after the treatment as untreated cells. This is correct only if
the treatment has no effect after it stops. The estimator also assumes that
the effect does not change with the earlier treatment periods. fasttrop gives
a warning message for a general design.

### Assumptions in the paper

The paper assumes no spillovers and no dynamic effects. TROP uses the cells of
the treated units before the treatment as untreated cells. Thus, the treatment
must not change outcomes before it starts. The treatment of one unit also must
not change the outcomes of other units. Outcomes can still change over time
for other reasons.

## The limits of this package

These limits apply to fasttrop 0.1.0:

- The package cannot use covariates.
- The global method works only for a block design, and it must have at least
  two units that are never treated.
- Outcomes can be `NA`, but the tests for the tuning and for the bootstrap use
  only a small number of `NA` cells.
- The equations come from arXiv version 3 of the paper. A line-by-line
  comparison with the journal version is not complete.
- We ran the validation scripts and the benchmark scripts only on Windows.
  GitHub Actions runs `R CMD check` on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

## Good practice

1. Make simulations that copy your data, and compare the methods on them.
   This is the preferred approach of the authors of TROP. The function
   `trop_simulate()` makes a simple panel. For a real check, the simulation
   must copy the patterns of your own data.
2. Compare TROP with TWFE. The article
   [How to read your results](read-your-results.html) shows how.
3. Make sure that the design that fasttrop reports is the design that you
   expect.
4. Use enough bootstrap draws for the final result. The default is 200.
5. Report the method, the tuning parameters, the number of treated units, the
   number of bootstrap draws, and the type of interval.
6. With few treated units, use the interval with care, and say so in your
   report.
